entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A rare, still-unexplained glowing ball that appears during thunderstorms, lasts a few seconds, and vanishes with or without leaving traces. The article treats it as a real but poorly documented atmospheric phenomenon, distinct from ordinary lightning strokes.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: A 19th-century French astronomer and physicist whose 1837 work on thunder, Sur le tonnerre, is credited with establishing the term for ball lightning used across European languages.

entries.name: Walther Brand
entries.background: A German school official who wrote Der Kugelblitz (1923), the only German-language monograph on ball lightning, compiling and reanalyzing older case reports such as Haidinger's.

entries.name: Martin A. Uman
entries.background: A leading American lightning researcher whose comprehensive lightning handbook (with Vladimir Rakov) is treated as the authoritative modern reference summarizing scientific knowledge and skepticism about ball lightning.

entries.name: COST Action P18
entries.background: A European-funded research collaboration proposal on the physics of lightning, involving about 30 researchers, whose consensus statement treated the reality of ball lightning as not in doubt.

entries.name: Prairie Meteorite Network
entries.background: A US network of cameras that continuously photographed the night sky for over a decade to track meteors, whose archives were later searched and yielded two probable chance captures of ball lightning.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.senseHere: The Austrian network of ground sensors that detects and locates individual lightning strokes, used in the article to cross-check witness reports of ball lightning against real recorded strikes.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.senseHere: The German counterpart to ALDIS, a lightning-location network used in the article to confirm the timing and strength of strokes associated with reported ball lightning sightings.

entries.name: cloud–ground stroke
entries.senseHere: A lightning discharge that connects a cloud to the ground, as distinguished in the article's statistics from strokes that stay within or between clouds and from the strokes' electrical polarity (positive or negative).

entries.name: Pyotr Leonidovich Kapitsa
entries.background: A Nobel Prize-winning Soviet physicist who proposed a theoretical mechanism for ball lightning without ever claiming to have personally witnessed the phenomenon.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: A 19th-century Austrian geologist and mineralogist at the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna who documented a detailed 1868 multi-witness ball lightning sighting across several city districts.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: A German astrophysicist who as a child witnessed a dramatic 1951 ball lightning event that fragmented into smaller spheres, later publishing a detailed scientific account with energy calculations.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: A British radio astronomer and later professor of physical electronics whose 1963 in-flight ball lightning sighting, published in Nature, became one of the most widely cited cases in the field.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: An 18th-century Baltic German physicist at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences who died in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity, an accident later mythologized in popular depictions as a ball lightning strike.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: A short-lived paralysis or numbness in a limb caused by a nearby lightning or ball lightning event, as opposed to longer-lasting psychological trauma from the same encounter.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: A pioneering French neurologist at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris, and a teacher of Sigmund Freud, known for studying the neurological aftereffects suffered by a patient who encountered ball lightning.

entries.name: triggered lightning
entries.senseHere: Lightning deliberately induced for research by launching a small rocket trailing a grounded wire into a thunderstorm, used at a Florida test site to study how lightning interacts with different ground materials.

entries.name: soil strike theory
aliases: Abrahamson and Dinniss soil strike theory
entries.senseHere: A proposed explanation that ball lightning forms when a lightning strike vaporizes soil minerals, producing a glowing cloud of burning metal and silicon particles; a 2012 spectrum matching this theory's predicted elements is cited as supporting evidence.

entries.name: slitless spectroscopy
entries.senseHere: A camera technique using a diffraction grating instead of a narrow slit to capture the spread of light wavelengths from a moving, unpredictable source like a ball lightning event, allowing its chemical composition to be read from the recorded colors.
